questions.prompt: Why must app servers be stateless before you can freely add more of them behind a load balancer?

options.text: So any server can handle any request, wherever the user's previous request went
Because load balancers can't send traffic to servers with memory
Because stateless servers use less CPU

questions.explanation: If a server keeps a user's data in its own memory, the next request must reach that same server. Moving state to a shared store lets any server handle any request.

questions.prompt: Some requests take 5 ms and others take 5 seconds. Which balancing algorithm keeps servers most evenly loaded?
questions.explanation: Round robin counts requests, not work, so a server can collect several slow requests. Least connections sends new work to the server with the fewest requests still in progress.

questions.prompt: You want /api/* to go to one pool of servers and /images/* to another. What kind of load balancer do you need?
questions.explanation: Routing by URL path requires reading the HTTP request, which only a layer 7 balancer does.

questions.prompt: Which steps remove the load balancer as a single point of failure? Select all that apply.

options.text: Run an active–passive pair sharing a floating IP
Use a managed cloud load balancer built from many machines
Give the single balancer more CPU
Spread users across several balancers or regions with DNS

questions.explanation: Redundancy removes the single point of failure. A bigger single machine is still one machine that can fail.

questions.prompt: Each server's health check also verifies the database connection. The database has a short outage. What risk does this create?

options.text: None; unhealthy servers should always be removed
Every server fails its check at once, the balancer removes them all, and the site is fully down even for pages that don't need the database
The health checks will overload the load balancer

questions.explanation: A shared dependency makes every check fail together, emptying the pool. Keep the routing check shallow (can this process serve?) and monitor dependencies separately, or let servers degrade gracefully.
